title: Right-angled cell walls arise because older walls solidify before new partitions form

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Right-angled cell walls arise because older walls solidify before new partitions form

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Plant cell walls often meet at right angles (Sachs’s Rule) because an earlier wall has usually become solid and rigid before a later partition joins it, so the fluid partition sets itself at equal angles, i.e. perpendicular, to the rigid wall.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: fluid partition meets a rigid wall at 90^\circ (Sachs's rule)

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: such validity as the rule possesses is due to the fact that among plant-tissues it very frequently happens that one cell-wall has become solid and rigid before another and later partition-wall is developed in connection with it.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter VII, “The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates”; topic “Three surfaces in contact and Sachs’s Rule”. Scope: plant tissues with rigid cell walls

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: fluid partition meets a rigid wall at 90^\circ (Sachs's rule)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch07-02: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.66

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The mechanism supplies a clear comparison based on wall age and rigidity. Existing imaging can establish timing and angles for some tissues, but paired mechanical data and broad plant coverage are incomplete.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure junction angles, relative wall age and stiffness, and division timing in plant tissues, testing whether new walls meet already rigid walls perpendicularly more often than equally young walls.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Geometry and division rules offer competing explanations for right angles.

Wall stiffness is rarely measured in the same time series.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.66
data existence: 0.62

operationalizability: 0.84
discriminating power: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The angle prediction is sharp, and meristem and embryo volumes contain the walls. What they lack for a full test is a direct marker that the older wall had solidified before the new one arrived. Angle-versus-sequence comparisons are feasible for Arabidopsis and remain a proxy for the rigidity mechanism across plants.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify plant-cell junctions by whether the older wall was already rigid when the new partition met it, and measure the angle. Right angles confined to rigid-wall meetings, with fluid-fluid meetings near 120 degrees, would support the claim; right angles between walls that were still fluid, or 120-degree meetings against already rigid walls, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Coverage is concentrated on Arabidopsis, not plant tissues at large.

Wall rigidity is usually inferred from age or cellulose signal rather than measured directly in these stacks.
